final_message:
All five versions are built and print exactly the expected output, byte for byte, on all four samples (`s1a`, `s1b`, `s2`, `s3`).

**Testing**
- I wrote a Python reference that follows SPEC.md directly (`test/ref.py`). It matches the samples, and I used it to make six more cases: a box with B = 1, an odd number of walkers, a huge B, zero steps, more walkers than workers, and seeds that wrap past 2^64.
- Every version passes all samples and extra cases with 1, 3, 16 and 32 workers.
- On a benchmark-size input (64 walkers × 500,000 steps, B = 300), all five print the same answer.
- Each version also has a slower fallback for boxes wider than its fast path allows, which needs billions of steps per walker (in JS, more than 16,384 steps and a box at least as wide). The real inputs never reach it, so I tested it by building copies with the fallback forced on; all passed.

**Algorithm (same in all five)**
- Threads take the next walker number from a shared atomic counter. Each walker's result goes into its own slot, and the slots are combined in walker order, so the output can't depend on the number of workers. The main thread does work too, so there are exactly WORKERS threads.
- Only the top two bits of each random number are used. The last step of the generator never changes them, so it is skipped.
- Both coordinates, shifted to start at B, are packed into one 64-bit word. A step is a bump only when the walker is already on the edge it is moving toward, so a bump is one masked compare against a small per-direction table. A return is one compare against the packed start position.
- A box wider than L behaves exactly like a box of size L, so B is capped at L.

**Speed choices per language**
- **C++:** branch-free hot loop using a table and conditional moves; `std::thread`. Stdout is set to binary so lines end in `\n`, not `\r\n`; before that fix the output differed from the samples. I also found that MSVC had turned two counters into a slow vector sequence that every step had to wait on, so I rewrote the loop to avoid it.
- **Java:** a separate method per kernel with branches, which suit the benchmark because bumps and returns are rare; plain `Thread`s with an `AtomicInteger`.
- **C#:** the hot method is marked to compile fully optimised straight away, and the tables are on the stack and read through pointers, so there are no bounds checks. In the `.csproj` I turned off the background garbage collector and the quick first-pass compile for methods with loops.
- **Go:** fixed-size arrays indexed by a value the compiler knows is 0–3, so it drops the bounds checks; goroutines with an atomic counter.
- **JS:** worker threads, with a shared memory buffer for the counter and results. The 64-bit generator is done in 32-bit halves with `Math.imul`, and the second multiply only computes the high word it needs. The two coordinates are packed into one 32-bit integer and the step logic has no branches. Each thread runs the kernel on a few tiny walks first. Without this, Node threw away the optimised loop at the end of every walk, and it ran about 40% slower.

**Rough timings on this machine** (benchmark size, best of 5; the machine was busy, so expect noise):

| | 1 worker | 16 workers |
|---|---|---|
| C++ | 72 ms | 22 ms |
| Go | 61 ms | 25 ms |
| C# | 127 ms | 96 ms |
| Java | 236 ms | 264 ms |
| JS | 441 ms | 247 ms |

Java gains nothing from 16 workers because JVM startup and compile time take up most of its run time.

The test files are in `test/`: `ref.py`, `check.sh`, `tm.py` (a timing script), the extra cases and `bench.in`.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
